body.heading: The Moon and the Sun start the week
paragraphs: Monday is the Moon's day — the name comes from Old English for 'day of the Moon' — and Sunday is plainly the Sun's day. Both follow an ancient pattern of naming days after the seven visible 'wanderers' of the sky: the Sun, the Moon, and the five planets visible to the naked eye.
That seven-day pattern travelled widely in the ancient world. The Romans named days for the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, and versions of that scheme spread across Europe.

body.heading: When Roman gods became Norse gods
paragraphs: As the names passed into Germanic languages, speakers swapped in their own gods for the Roman ones. Mars, the Roman god of war, became Tiw (Tyr) — giving Tuesday. Mercury's day became Woden's, or Odin's, day: Wednesday.

Jupiter, the Roman thunder god, was matched with Thor, the Norse thunder god — Thursday. Venus's day became Frigg's or Freyja's day: Friday. Only Saturn kept his Roman name in English, which is why Saturday sounds different from the rest.

body.heading: Other languages kept other clues
paragraphs: In French, Spanish, and Italian, the Roman originals are easier to spot: mardi and martes still carry Mars, and mercredi and miércoles still carry Mercury. In those languages, Sunday often became 'the Lord's day' instead of the Sun's.
So an ordinary week quietly preserves ancient astronomy and two pantheons of gods. Every calendar appointment you make is scheduled, in part, by mythology.

takeaway: Weekday names preserve an ancient sky-watchers' system: Sun and Moon days, Roman planet-gods, and Norse swaps that gave us Tiw's, Woden's, Thor's, and Frigg's days.
